output.text:
☀️ Weekly Summary

We welcomed new members this week. Members shared a completed walnut sideboard, a first café-stool commission, a student’s steam-bent ash chair and progress on a cherry writing desk. The liveliest technical discussion covered clamping a five-board oak top: use clamps every 20–25 cm, alternate them above and below with cauls, and ensure the boards are properly acclimated and closely matched in moisture. Coming up: the monthly video call is next Thursday at 19:00 Paris time, and the Lyon meet-up is on Saturday 10 October at 10am in Villeurbanne.

🙌 New members

  • Aurélie Brunet is a cabinetmaker making kitchen and dining furniture in a two-person workshop near Nantes, France, mainly in oak and ash. She joined to seek a second opinion on pricing her first large commission on her own before sending the quote.
  • Tomasz Wierzbicki is a joiner in Bristol, UK, making staircases and window frames for renovation work and beginning to build small tables in the evenings. He is happy to answer questions about stairs.
  • Nadia Haddad teaches adult woodworking classes and builds chairs in Montréal, Quebec, with a focus on steam-bending. She is looking to swap offcuts and for ideas on keeping beginners safe on the bandsaw.
  • Olumide Adeyemi is a final-year furniture design student in Lyon, France, on placement at a small workshop until December. He joined to learn about pricing, quoting and finding clients, and plans to share his graduation piece when it is finished.

show-your-work

Karin Lindqvist finished a walnut sideboard for the couple she mentioned last month, with four doors, a sliding-dovetail carcass and hand-cut finger pulls. It took 61 hours, nine more than quoted, mostly on the doors; in response to Samuel Okafor's question about the grain match, Karin said she resawn and bookmatched one 60 mm board she had saved for two years.

Hugo Martel shared his first commission from the market stall: six oak stools for a bakery café. The owner's requirement that they stack made the leg splay a puzzle.

Nadia Haddad shared a student's first chair from her autumn class. Made from ash with a steam-bent back, the student completed every joint herself.

Priya Raman shared progress on a cherry writing desk, with the drawer boxes glued up. She used hand-cut half-blind dovetails on the fronts and machine-cut joints on the backs.

techniques

Tomasz Wierzbicki asked how to clamp a 90 cm oak top made from five boards after his last one cupped. Karin Lindqvist, Samuel Okafor and Priya Raman recommended clamps every 20–25 cm, alternating above and below with end cauls; matching board moisture, allowing at least three weeks’ stickered acclimation in autumn, aiming for boards within 1 percent of each other and 8–10 percent for indoor furniture, and alternating growth rings when appearance allows. Tomasz said he had not checked the moisture and had left the boards in the workshop for a week.

Olumide Adeyemi asked how far to offset the peg hole when drawboring the mortise-and-tenon joints on his graduation bench. Hugo Martel recommended about 1.5 mm in oak for a 10 mm peg, warning that more than 2 mm can split the tenon cheek or snap the peg, and suggested making a test joint from offcuts of the same board.

finishing

Aurélie Brunet asked why hardwax oil on the underside of a table was still tacky after three days in a 12°C workshop. Karin Lindqvist said cold temperatures below 15°C slow curing and excess oil left on the surface is usually the cause, advising one very thin coat and a firm wipe after 20 minutes; Nadia Haddad suggested shellac for small winter projects, while noting it is unsuitable for dining tables because of water and heat. Aurélie wiped the oil back hard and moved the table into the house, where it was dry by the next morning.

tools-and-sharpening

Olumide Adeyemi asked about bench-chisel sharpening angles after receiving 25° and 30° advice. Samuel Okafor said a 25° primary bevel with a 30° microbevel suits most work, with steeper angles for chopping hardwood mortises and shallower ones for paring softwood.

Hugo Martel said that after a month without a honing guide, his edges had become rounder. He is going back to using the guide.

Tomasz Wierzbicki is giving away eight old 250 mm table saw blades, most still sharp, after switching to a track saw for sheet goods. They are free to anyone in the Bristol hub who can collect.

commissions-and-pricing

Aurélie Brunet asked whether a €4,800 quote for a solid oak extending dining table, from 180 cm to 240 cm for a family of six, was realistic given €1,150 in timber and hardware and an estimated 70 hours. Karin Lindqvist, Hugo Martel and Priya Raman advised calculating a sustainable hourly rate including overheads and unpaid work, pricing the extension mechanism separately, and setting clear limits on included design revisions; Aurélie recalculated to €5,900 with design included and the mechanism as its own line, and planned to send the quote tomorrow.

sawdust-lounge

Samuel Okafor found a 1950s hand plane at a car boot sale for 4 pounds; it needs a new iron and a lot of love. Hugo Martel backed Samuel’s view that there is no such thing as enough planes—only not enough wall.

Priya Raman reminded members that the monthly video call is next Thursday at 19:00 Paris time. The topic is how each person handles a client who changes the design after the timber is cut.

🌎 Geographic hubs

🇫🇷-lyon

Julien Ferrand announced this month’s meet-up on Saturday 10 October at 10am in his workshop in Villeurbanne, with a sharpening demonstration and coffee. Attendance is limited to 12; Olumide Adeyemi said he will come and can follow the demonstration despite his French still being slow.

Julien Ferrand said the group oak order has reached 3 m³, and the sawmill will deliver on 21 October. There is still space for about 0.5 m³ for anyone who would like to join.

🇬🇧-bristol

Tomasz Wierzbicki said that four people are sharing a van to the timber yard on the 17th, with room for one more order if it fits in a 3-metre bed. Samuel Okafor took up the space for a few ash boards for chair legs and offered to bring coffee.

🇨🇦-montreal

Nadia Haddad announced that her January evening course is full and has opened a waiting list. She asked for ash offcuts longer than 60 cm for bending exercises, and Émile Tremblay will drop off around ten 70 cm offcuts on Thursday.
